comments.body: This analysis is a bit absurd.  It includes in its premise that the debate about affordability is due to near term inflation that has been recently experienced.  Sure, that exists but the frank reality is that when I discuss it among my peers it is that huge structural things have shifted.  The cost of homes, education and medical care all can grow and change over time in ways that are disconnected to what we earn.  My kid will face a 20’s with more debt as he becomes an adult when I did and a basic home in our area will be a factor of 2 or 3 times more than his expected starting income than I faced. As an older person, I’m looking at a medical world where there is no coherence in what things cost and there is no reasonable way for me to navigate/mitigate those expenses.  The layers of players in the middle who jack up drug prices and an impossible insurance bureaucracy make me feel incapable of “shopping” by price or negotiating my medical expenses.   These are long term structural changes that make our world feel less affordable than when we were young and fear for what our kids are inheriting.  This doesn’t even touch on the mountain of government debt that will come due some day as well.  It all leads to one phrase.  Eat the rich.

Writing is a fundamental and vital skill. And, judging by the obvious decay in basic skills, Americans are rapidly losing the ability to do it. This trend threatens our ability to communicate with each other.

Schools need to ban all forms of technology in the classroom. And all written assignments must be done by handwriting only and in class. Otherwise, you can be sure that students will use AI.

But that won't be enough. Writing is a form of thinking, a way to make sense of new information, and a tool for learning in addition to a mode of expression. So it must be integrated into every subject in every classroom. 

Kids must again be taught how to build sentences, how to distinguish between verbs and nouns and adjectives and other forms, and, yes, how to spell. And we must hold them to a grade-appropriate standard that moves away from the "writing does not matter" ethos that has dominated our education system for 30 years or so.

comments.name: Jack

I have taught writing (composition) for over 50 years--high-school, university, overseas: even such career writing as technical, business, medical writing.  I am convinced that writing is the single-most  difficult task in any workplace.

It requires  language skills: grammar, diction, usage, etc.

It requires logic skills: beginning, middle end, and a multtiude of sidetracks.  Cause and effect. Deifnition of terms.

It requires audience: Who? When? Prior knowledge.  Teacher?  Colleague?  Boss?  President? 

Interpersonal skills : Purpose, persuasion?

It requires intrapersonal skills: voice, voices, personal growth, fear?

It requires an ear: What Do I sound like?  Is it me?   Can anyone read it aloud.  Should it be read aloud?

It requires a sense of space: What does it look like on paper, in a meme, on a tract or brochure?

And writing gives us a chance to put down our thoughts for a moment to re-read, reflect, and revise.  It hones our thoughts.

And we get to do this in a freshman composition course, or in a memo, or in an address to Congress.

Keep on writing people.

I'm a retired academic and served on a number of search committees. Typically a search committee does the vetting of a pool of applicants.

The first cut is usually closes the pool forming a group that is "qualified" for the position. Then the second cut decides who to interview. The third step involves selecting from this now much smaller group who to recommend.

Some systems ask for a ranking of those recommended. Others don't. Ultimately the decision to make an offer is made by the Provost or President. But as a practical matter, most President's rely on their faculty to have conducted a rigorous process and follow their recommendation.

But despite this process subjective judgements enter the deliberations at every stage. And this is where things can go terribly wrong.

From this article it appears that Cambridge passed over two well qualified Black women to choose a candidate that would serve as a showpiece, a rags to riches cocktail party discussion accomplishment certifying the liberal character of the institution.

How or why did this happen? Because we do not have a reliable method of uncovering our own biasses during this process and putting them in check.

I’m a power-systems engineer specialising in transmission reliability and grid restoration. I started my career in Britain, working on contingency planning for major grid failure.

Britain gets one thing right: it treats a nationwide blackout as something you plan for. The system is more centrally coordinated and has explicit restoration arrangements: restart generators, build electrical “islands,” restore critical infrastructure and reconnect the network progressively.

I moved to the US more than a decade ago and have spent much of that time trying to convince utilities, regulators and lawmakers that America is far too complacent about the same risk.

The US grid is vastly larger and more fragmented, while some critical transformers weigh hundreds of tonnes and can take years to replace.

America is good at dealing with outages, but it is simply unprepared for an adversary deliberately destroying the equipment needed to bring the grid back. It's a very real problem we might have to face but we spend pretty much no time thinking about it.

In this story, for example, we see that the steel at the heart of America's power grid is only manufactured at a single plant in the United States. The transformers upon which the grid relies have a 128 week lead time. 

And the power grid issues outlined here are just one factor of the problem. This country seems less and less able to build, well, anything, on time and on budget these days. Ships, medicines, housing, infrastructure, transformers - how this can be viewed as anything but an epic failure of long term, strategic planning is a mystery to me. There is an urgent need, for reasons of national security if nothing else, to revitalize American building and manufacturing, and to build resiliency within both our society and economy.

I believe it may be time for the public at large to:
1. Do not instantly dismiss someone who has a big list of self diagnosed mental issues, as they probably are in actual distress about life.
2. Start demanding actual evidence for these "disorders." If none is provided, we as a society should reject the idea that the behaviors or emotions at hand are "medical disorders" at all. We need to be honest about the fact that psychology has essentially medicalized most feelings, states of mind, etc. Your kid doesn't pay attention in school? Well it's not because you're not involved in their education enough, or that your kid isn't very bright, or they don't care about school cause it's boring and they're a kid. It's really because they have ADD, ADHD, they have clinical anxiety, they have whatever. Not one of these things has any hard evidence to prove its existence, but each one does offer an explanation without blame, a highly sought after status of victimhood, and an immediate obligation on the part of society to cater to the person who has the supposed illness.

I thought the article was insightful in many ways, but my conclusion is wildly different. It makes more sense to me to dismiss most of these diagnoses (whether they are self diagnosed or diagnosed by a psychiatrist) until we start getting some biological evidence of these disorders (which psychiatrists have been promising were just around the corner since the 1980's). Demanding proof will end most of this.

That's not to say that a lot of kids don't have real psychological issues. And of course, it is important that people (young and old) seek help when they need it, without fear of being stigmatized. 

But for many people (and here I would include adults as well as young people), overthinking it just leads to overdiagnosis. If I think about it, hey, I worry a lot,  I must have anxiety disorder. And I feel sad and hopeless at times. Gee, I must suffer from depression. And sometimes I have trouble focusing. It must be ADHD!  Those conditions are certainly real in some cases, and I don't in any way mean to disparage those who suffer from them. But I think applying those labels to the normal emotional speed bumps that occur in any life can actually make matters worse.

comments.name: David Messineo
comments.body:
I strongly believe in ABC's First Amendment rights. But ABC is private; the broadcast spectrum it uses is not. If we really wanted to work this out rather than make it another fight over Trump, ABC or the FCC, here's one approach.

Make public access a condition of every broadcast license. Give the sitting administration fixed airtime each week—say one prime-time and one non-prime-time hour. The administration controls the content; the network identifies it as such without endorsing it.

Licensees could also fund something like C-SPAN: a public political channel with time controlled by the Democratic and Republican parties, plus time allocated independently of either party through neutral rules and a lottery. "Independent" describes the allocation, not political affiliation.

No FCC official decides whether ABC was fair. No counting positive and negative stories. No government review of its journalism. ABC remains free to criticize, investigate and report however it chooses.

But protecting ABC's speech doesn't mean an unconditional right to use a scarce public resource however it chooses. A broadcast license can carry reasonable, viewpoint-neutral public-access conditions. If ABC believes only it can decide how it uses the public's airwaves, perhaps it shouldn't have the license.

comments.name: Jim Caruso
comments.body:
I have always believed that writing is thinking. It helps you clarify thoughts. As Ms. Stanger so eloquently says, “writing is a means to learning who you are and what you value,” and “Writing is thinking made visible: The sentence that resists you does so because the thought inside it is unfinished.”

For these reasons, I avoid using AI much in my writing, except for certain business applications, like compressing complexities into succinct bullet points for board meeting PowerPoints, and the assessment of tone in certain emails when I know the topic makes me angry or defensive.

But Ms. Stanger hasconvinced me that there’s a place for AI in creative writing too. In some ways it can be just a natural extension of the thesaurus function in Microsoft Word - helping to rephrase a sentence instead of just substituting a word. Any book you read is not solely the author’s words - it has had extensive input from an editor - so for those of us who are not published authors, AI can be our editors.

I think Ms. Stanger has identified the right boundaries and guardrails. The only point I might debate is “the structural diagnosis of a chapter that won’t cohere” - isn’t part of the process of “writing as thinking” to figure out the proper structure?

All I know is that, as a part-time author of fiction, the publishing agents I’ve approached have warned not to use AI to help you write, in terms of style, grammar and all that. If they think you’re using it, they won’t bother considering what you have to offer.

Think of it…if everybody used AI in the way they write, it could be hard to detect any plagiarism. How can you accuse someone of copying from someone else if they’re all using AI? How can you defend you own original works as being original and unique if others seem to write the same way you do, word for word, if we all use AI?  

Better to write in your own writing style than to use AI’s style. As an aside, Bret Stephens, who used to write in this op-ed section for the WSJ, wrote in the NY Times that he is against writing using AI.

comments.name: Jim Fini
comments.body: Great article that I agree with. Creative endeavors of all stripes, whether it is a novel, a blog post, Art, music or starting companies, all begin with an idea that a structure.  That spark can only come from humans. Within that framework, artificial intelligence, it’s like having an army of analysts and editors that can help improve the final product. And isn’t the final product the goal?

comments.name: Donald Ross
comments.body: Tolstoy seemed to do alright without it. Solzhenitsyn did alright from a prison cell. Bronte got it from her mind, not a machine. The above is a lame excuse for laziness. I absolutely enjoy the process of writing, researching, and re-writing all by myself. It's not like we are too busy now that we have AI but somehow good writers did well before.

comments.name: John Borrillo
comments.body: I taught writing at the college level for decades and had to compete , unsuccessfully , with various fashions and fads. The first and most indelible  was the move from in-class essays written in blue books  to having students write their assignments in computer labs. The focus was on computer operations and the gloss of “cutting edge” technology and not on actual learning. The result was a loss of  educational focus and a plummeting of academic standards.  AI is the latest techno fad that encourages second-hand thinking,  passivity and dependency by way of a fallacious appeal to authority. It is yet another mass delusion.

comments.name: Christine Summerson
comments.body: I would argue that you are making AI a better writer. through your interactions.

comments.name: Alan Compagnon
comments.body: As many have stated, Saint Malo has way too many tourists in general, especially in the summer. Off season it’s manageable and worth the visit just for Vauban. There are many other places en Bretagne that are far more charming. One more thing: Bretagne is rightfully associated with its vast coastline, which extends from the Morbihan in the southwest to the Cote d’Emeraude in the northeast. Most of Brittany is the agricultural interior, consisting of livestock based agriculture (corn, wheat, sorghum, etc.) and numerous huge pig farms. Sadly, much of coastal Brittany is polluted by the agricultural industry and pig farms that dominate the region’s economy. The coast of Brittany is magical indeed but not without problems. Chief among those problems is coastal water quality—many beaches are unhealthy for swimming and collecting shellfish. France publishes a map showing every beach in the country and the water quality for each.

comments.name: Uji10jo
comments.body:
Cancale's oysters! YES! We had dozens. Nice break for a quiet lunch after Mont-Saint Michel.
A statue of Samuel Champlain, who founded Quebec, Canada, is there. He had a strong tie with Saint-Malo, a fortified town with massive ramparts.

comments.name: Frank
comments.body:
I spent a day being driven around by a group of young French people in 1982 or 1983 - we went to Cap Fréhel, where I was amazed to be standing just feet away from an inaccessible cliff-top island covered with thousands of nesting seabirds comfortable in their awareness that despite humans gawping at them from some feet way - the precipitous drop to the rocky seabed between meant they were completely safe.

We then went to view what I thought was Mont St. Michel, but I remember wondering why I didn't see a spike or spire as in the famous images I had seen of it.  We then got riotously drunk that evening in a closed seaside pub/restaurant, and I forget the rest.

I have repeatedly checked for other built-on islands in the area: St.Malo, Grand Bé, Fort National, but none quite match what I remembered seeing.

So I'm left wondering - did Mont St. Michel, around 1982-1983, have the pointy spire removed for renovations?  Or did I just see another similar but slightly less impressive built-up island in the St. Malo area?

comments.name: Theresa
comments.body: The article mentioned the reporter visited early this summer. Considering that, and viewing photos of folks in Cancale wearing heavy jackets, it seems the reporter avoided this summer’s canicules. Future visitors should know that we just wrapped up our fifth heatwave. Temperatures where I live hit as high as 106F. We now have drought conditions, water restrictions and fears about how this area can manage a future of global warming.

comments.body: Our family group rafted the Colorado River in 2016 with WRE.  What a trip.  My younger brother and I took water proof Olympus cameras and each shot 200 photos. I had done 6 other books on our RV travels to Alaska and about 48 states.  Almost forgot, I had a heart attack in January 2016--recovered and enjoyed the rafting!

comments.body: What the trip gives you is perspective as you look at the layers of rock and the millions of years they represent, day after day. Human beings are a blink of history on that scale and always will be. We're simply not that important and the planet knows that, even if we don't.

Get out there!!

comments.name: Edie Clark
comments.body: Nothing like it. Our 13 day trip with guides paddling oar rafts was life changing. Once you are out of sight of Navajo Bridge, civilization is gone. No motors, no phones, it’s so quiet. We camped on sandbars each night, no need for tents. Your senses become acutely attuned to your surroundings. The descending trill of a Canyon Wren , the shadow of a giant condor circling high above, the rippling of the river that lulls you to sleep at night. Waking up just before dawn to see bats circling above you against a background of  billions of stars. We stopped briefly at Phantom Ranch, where tourists  arriving on mules can stay overnight in stone cabins. After a week on the river, the taste of a lemonade with ice (!) was incredible . One day the monsoons began, and it rained somewhere in the desert high above us, and we witnessed something few have seen- over two dozen ephemeral waterfalls, plunging from high above us, turning the river red with sediment. After all, it is named the Colorado. Go. Before it is too late.

articles.title: Rafting a River in Flux Through the Grand Canyon

comments.name: Peas Corps
comments.body: I unapologetically love Les Mis, but of course theaters cannot and should not constantly present the same hits over and over. Being part of a choral organization for many years, I understand firsthand that performing well-loved pieces is what brings in the money so you can then perform and bring to light lesser known works. Christmas concerts and the Mozart, Verdi and Brahms Requiems pay the bills for choirs. The Nutcracker pays the bills for ballet organizations. Our hope is that people who have a great experience at these pop performances will then be moved to return to hear an unfamiliar piece and eventually buy season tix.

comments.name: Paul
comments.body: I have seen this show in London and on screen. It is magnificent. As a former actor/singer I deeply regret that I never had a chance to perform in it. The only drawback is that it requires elaborate staging and a full orchestra which puts it out of range for many amateur theaters. Still, it's inspiring.

comments.name: Cathy
comments.body: The themes of Les Mis are universal and never fail to resonate as does the soaring music.  “Do you hear the people sing” has become a standard for protest groups and is never more relevant than today when there is so much to protest. Most people recognize the music of The Phantom but not many can sing along with it.  There is something about the plaintive score and stirring story of injustice that people love.  Victor Hugo’s story of cruelty to the poor, the harsh judgment of the legal system and the bravery of an honest man that really speaks to people.

comments.name: Scott
comments.body: Sheesh.  How can I express my love of this show?  I have seen it many times and it moves me every time.  I play the tunes on piano constantly and never got tired of them.  If I was condemned to watching only one show for all eternity...this is it. It's sheer magic on stage. But...never, ever, ever, let Russel Crowe sing those songs again.

comments.name: LM
comments.body: I fell in love with an animated film version of “Les Miserables” (in French, my mother tongue) at the ripe old age of 7. The story captivated me. I then caught the musical for the first time at age 14 on Broadway and went on to see it 11 times (ten times on Broadway, once in London). The Radio City Show was fabulous. I am lucky to be able to read Victor Hugo’s novel in its original language. It’s my all time favorite book. It’s one of those stories that either gets deep under your skin or bores you silly. I’ve never met anyone who thought it was “so-so”.

comments.name: Shekhar
comments.body: The fact is Modi has ruined the Indian economy through a series of reckless decisions  - Invalidating 86% of the currency in circulation, implementation of country wide GST and a draconian shutdown during Covid. All these decisions, by all accounts, were taken without much consultation anong concerned parties. Collectively, these decisions have led to the loss of millions of jobs in informal small and medium sized companies, which generate the maximum employment in India. As many as 10 million workers lost their jobs and returned to their ancestral farms, creating extra mouths to feed, not extra hands to work. The economy has never recovered since then. This is the origin of youth unemployment and stagnating wages.

comments.name: R C
comments.body:
Let's ask American college-age kids how this makes them feel. Oh, they've sent back a meme. It's Jeremy Clarkson's "Oh no... anyway."

Thieves have turned "higher education" into a confidence game and H.L Mencken's people are hard up against the con. This has happened everywhere to some extent, even in countries like Denmark where the government pays college tuition, room, and board. The difference is if your "institution of learning" doesn't produce job-holding graduates, it gets shut down in Denmark.

People need to wise up. College degrees are a grift for 80% of the population. I use the liberal arts side of my collegiate education a lot more than the maths and sciences side in my day-to-day... and I work in STEM.

The problem with apprenticeships is that it's very hard to extract value from them as a middle man. College, on the other hand, is a highly profitable extraction tool.

Everywhere else on the planet, there will be higher unemployment than recent history of last 50 years. Neither the left nor the right leaning parties are listening. One party wants to keep importing people into the US. Those who say join the trades like plumbers, electricians, welders, etc. are probably correct while data-center construction is booming but once that stops or hits a plateau, there will be glut of those skills.

comments.name: Ignacio Götz
comments.body: While I lived in India from the 50s on, I was associated with St. Xavier's College in Mumbai and in Ahmedabad and in Kolkata, all private universities, Jesuit-run, and quite prestigious. But I had noticed that, in India, the old Hindu traditions of learning for its own sake -- because learning is one of the accepted paths (marg) to enlightenment -- was still a legitimate answer to questions of employment, which were raised then as they are now. Gyana-yoga is one of the paths taught by Sri Krishna to Arjuna in the "Bhagavadgita," and it is today carried out in other private universities, like Shanti-Vedanta, founded by Sri  Aurobindo, and Sayajirao University in Vadodara. Indians confront learning differently from Americans, because they have traditions that go back thousands of years, when associations of gurus and chelas dotted the forests during the "brahmacharya" life stage. Perhaps there is need to remember such traditions.

comments.name: Const
comments.body: Over the past two years, the hospital I work for has been offshoring technology jobs, often to India. Interestingly, many of the jobs being moved overseas were previously held by people who had themselves immigrated from India to the United States. It’s a reminder that even highly educated workers can find themselves caught in a global labor market where the jobs they trained for are increasingly being moved wherever labor is cheaper. And the next step may be even more disruptive: those jobs being moved from India to AI.

comments.name: Keith Lorigan

comments.name: curt gervelis
comments.body:
Great video and very informative.  A few questions / observations:

No real details about what Space Force (SF) capabilities were destroyed  during Epic Fury.

US leads in rocket launch capabilities thanks to Musk and SpaceX not NASA or the defense department.

During the AI discussion Saltzman made it clear that there will always be a "human in the loop" but the definition of what that means is not always clear.

The discussion about GPS is interesting but the US GPS system has been around for a long time and is antiquated in comparison to China's and its easy to jam so alternative technologies and solutions are very much needed.  Not much as revealed about what these could be or supported.

Good discussion about training as it is an important part of military operations that is often overlooked.  Simulations are a great way to address this need.

2027 military budget was mentioned but no actual numbers or amounts of money were provided.  Given the $1.4 T proposal for next year what amount is SF asking for and will it be approved?

I am curious about the JADC2 program and how SF will be involved if not one of the key agencies to support this program.

A fan at first but in fact huge overhead - 28 Flag officers for a force of 5300 enlisted and 4500 officers; all these functions were performed previously by National Agencies or USAF-Space (contractors too).

The die is cast and we have Space Force (distinct from Space Command), and USSF may eventually reach its potential through it's Joint training and operations with USAF, NGA and NRO - it is nascent currently.

USSF does do a phenomenal job of PR and advertising though, while the others prefer to fly below the radar even in non-classified aspects of the missions.

comments.body: We live in a country in which almost the whole world is vibrantly present in our choice of cuisines. Small places and big places. In small cities and big cities. There's not a state in this country, probably not even a county in this country that doesn't have some representation of a cuisine born elsewhere then brought here. And we're finally getting examples of the food that existed here on this land before this country was even a dream. Not every place is as excellent as Yerord Mas, of course, but that doesn't detract from the sheer abundance of variety. All of this, all of this pleasure we derive from elsewhere, and yet, as a country--because of the powers that be (not every individual needless to say)--we are retrenching, pulling away from the rest of the world, thumbing our nose at it. If only we could be guided by the grand global community of food, instead of all the other things that propel politics. We need places like Yerord Mas and people like Mr. Grigoryan. We need more and more. We need to sit down at the table with the rest of the world. Not just for dinner now and again, but for every meal. Expanding our food horizons should help us expand all our horizons. Unfortunately, it doesn't enough yet. Maybe that's because too many (we all know of some) who are wedded to the corporate food that the US exports and are blind to the joys of bringing goods and traditions and people from elsewhere  into this country. I wish we would learn! Maybe Yerord Mas will help.

I was a graduate student at Texas Tech in the 1990s and taking a Victorian literature course. The instructor was a conservative Christian deacon who took a casual poll during class, based on a document that I suspect was from the Heritage Foundation or other Republican think tank. The questions concerned a return to "the classics," the traditional literary canon during a time when postmodern critical approaches were on the rise. Most in class saw the benefit of studying the canon. I myself wrote a masters thesis on the English Puritan Commonwealth and its influence on Daniel Defoe, but I did frame the study using postmodern approaches. There are benefits in balancing the postmodern and the traditional.

But Creighton's ideology about sexuality and gender simply defies science. This is enormously troubling. Literature reflects the times, and if authors are addressing sexuality and gender in fiction and factually-based writings, this benefits society. It's distressing to see faculty flee TTU; but it's inevitable if Trumpy restrictions hamper freethought. imagination, and honest research that is peer-reviewed.

comments.name: C In NY
comments.body:
Data centers should be required to provide their own electricity rather than shifting the cost of their enormous power demands onto the existing electrical grid. When a data center creates a massive new demand for electricity, utilities must invest in additional generation, transmission, and distribution infrastructure—and those costs are ultimately borne by all ratepayers. Residential customers should not be forced to subsidize highly profitable data centers through higher electric bills. If these facilities need extraordinary amounts of power, they should be responsible for providing and paying for the additional generation and infrastructure required to serve them.

No data center should be approved unless it shows how it can provide its own power and cooling.
